stem:
Given below are some examples of wave motion. State in each case if the wave motion is transverse, longitudinal or a combination of both:

(a) Motion of a kink in a longitudinal spring produced by displacing one end of the spring sideways.

(b) Waves produced in a cylinder containing a liquid by moving its piston back and forth.

(c) Waves produced by a motorboat sailing in water.

(d) Ultrasonic waves in air produced by a vibrating quartz crystal.
solution:
(a) Transverse and longitudinal

(b) Longitudinal

(c) Transverse and longitudinal

(d) Longitudinal

subtopic: Displacement Relation in a Progressive Wave
stem:
A wave travelling along a string is described by,

\(y(x,\,t) = 0.005 \sin (80.0\,x - 3.0\,t)\),

in which the numerical constants are in SI units (\(0.005\,\text{m}\), \(80.0\,\text{rad m}^{-1}\), and \(3.0\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\)). Calculate (a) the amplitude, (b) the wavelength, and (c) the period and frequency of the wave. Also, calculate the displacement \(y\) of the wave at a distance \(x = 30.0\,\text{cm}\) and time \(t = 20\,\text{s}\) ?
solution:
On comparing this displacement equation with Eq. (14.2),

\(y(x,\,t) = a \sin (kx - \omega t)\),

we find

(a) the amplitude of the wave is \(0.005\,\text{m} = 5\,\text{mm}\).

(b) the angular wave number \(k\) and angular frequency \(\omega\) are

\(k = 80.0\,\text{m}^{-1}\) and \(\omega = 3.0\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

We, then, relate the wavelength \(\lambda\) to \(k\) through Eq. (14.6),

\(\lambda = 2\pi/k = \dfrac{2\pi}{80.0\,\text{m}^{-1}} = 7.85\,\text{cm}\)

(c) Now, we relate \(T\) to \(\omega\) by the relation

\(T = 2\pi/\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{3.0\,\text{s}^{-1}} = 2.09\,\text{s}\)

and frequency, \(\nu = 1/T = 0.48\,\text{Hz}\)

The displacement \(y\) at \(x = 30.0\,\text{cm}\) and time \(t = 20\,\text{s}\) is given by

\(y = (0.005\,\text{m})\sin (80.0 \times 0.3 - 3.0 \times 20)\)

\(= (0.005\,\text{m})\sin (-36 + 12\pi)\)

\(= (0.005\,\text{m})\sin (1.699)\)

\(= (0.005\,\text{m})\sin (97^{\circ}) \simeq 5\,\text{mm}\)

subtopic: The Speed of a Travelling Wave
stem: A steel wire \(0.72\,\text{m}\) long has a mass of \(5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\). If the wire is under a tension of \(60\,\text{N}\), what is the speed of transverse waves on the wire ?
solution:
Mass per unit length of the wire,

\(\mu = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}}{0.72\,\text{m}} = 6.9 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\)

Tension, \(T = 60\,\text{N}\)

The speed of wave on the wire is given by

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{60\,\text{N}}{6.9 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg m}^{-1}}} = 93\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

subtopic: The Speed of a Travelling Wave
stem: Estimate the speed of sound in air at standard temperature and pressure. The mass of \(1\) mole of air is \(29.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\).
solution:
We know that \(1\) mole of any gas occupies \(22.4\) litres at STP. Therefore, density of air at STP is:

\(\rho_{o} =\) (mass of one mole of air) / (volume of one mole of air at STP)

\(= \dfrac{29.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}}{22.4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{3}} = 1.29\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)

According to Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a medium, we get for the speed of sound in air at STP,

\(v = \left[\dfrac{1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{-2}}{1.29\,\text{kg m}^{-3}}\right]^{1/2} = 280\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
_note: The chapter immediately observes that this Newtonian estimate is about 15% below the measured 331 m/s, and that the Laplace correction (v = sqrt(gamma P / rho), gamma = 7/5) raises it to 331.3 m/s. The printed 280 m/s is therefore deliberate, not an error.

subtopic: Superposition of Waves and Standing Waves
stem: A pipe, \(30.0\,\text{cm}\) long, is open at both ends. Which harmonic mode of the pipe resonates a \(1.1\,\text{kHz}\) source? Will resonance with the same source be observed if one end of the pipe is closed ? Take the speed of sound in air as \(330\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
solution:
The first harmonic frequency is given by

\(\nu_{1} = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_{1}} = \dfrac{v}{2L}\)  (open pipe)

where \(L\) is the length of the pipe. The frequency of its \(n\)th harmonic is:

\(\nu_{n} = \dfrac{nv}{2L}\), for \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\) (open pipe)

First few modes of an open pipe are shown in Fig. 14.15.

For \(L = 30.0\,\text{cm}\), \(v = 330\,\text{m s}^{-1}\),

\(\nu_{n} = \dfrac{n\,330\,(\text{m s}^{-1})}{0.6\,(\text{m})} = 550\,n\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Clearly, a source of frequency \(1.1\,\text{kHz}\) will resonate at \(\nu_{2}\), i.e. the second harmonic.

Now if one end of the pipe is closed (Fig. 14.15), it follows from Eq. (14.15) that the fundamental frequency is

\(\nu_{1} = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_{1}} = \dfrac{v}{4L}\)  (pipe closed at one end)

and only the odd numbered harmonics are present :

\(\nu_{3} = \dfrac{3v}{4L}\), \(\nu_{5} = \dfrac{5v}{4L}\), and so on.

For \(L = 30\,\text{cm}\) and \(v = 330\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the fundamental frequency of the pipe closed at one end is \(275\,\text{Hz}\) and the source frequency corresponds to its fourth harmonic. Since this harmonic is not a possible mode, no resonance will be observed with the source, the moment one end is closed.
_note: TWO printed cross-references in this solution look wrong and are transcribed faithfully. (1) The closed-pipe paragraph cites 'Fig. 14.15', but Fig. 14.15 is the OPEN-pipe figure; the closed-at-one-end modes are Fig. 14.14. (2) It cites 'Eq. (14.15)' for the closed-pipe fundamental, but Eq. (14.15) is lambda = v/nu; the closed-pipe normal modes are Eq. (14.44) with n = 0. Neither affects the numerical answer.

stem: Two sitar strings A and B playing the note 'Dha' are slightly out of tune and produce beats of frequency \(5\,\text{Hz}\). The tension of the string B is slightly increased and the beat frequency is found to decrease to \(3\,\text{Hz}\). What is the original frequency of B if the frequency of A is \(427\,\text{Hz}\) ?
solution:
Increase in the tension of a string increases its frequency. If the original frequency of B (\(
u_{B}\)) were greater than that of A (\(
u_{A}\)), further increase in \(
u_{B}\) should have resulted in an increase in the beat frequency. But the beat frequency is found to decrease. This shows that \(
u_{B} < 
u_{A}\). Since \(
u_{A} - 
u_{B} = 5\,	ext{Hz}\), and \(
u_{A} = 427\,	ext{Hz}\), we get \(
u_{B} = 422\,	ext{Hz}\).
